factor-markets-s2.title: Welders at the Brackwater boatyards
factor-markets-s2.html: Brackwater is an invented harbor town where several boatyards build small fishing boats. Each boat needs many hours of welding. This year a new fish-processing plant opens nearby, and local fishing crews want more boats. The boatyards begin looking for more welders, and the welders' union reports that boatyards are offering more hours.

factor-demand-supply-s3.title: A year in the invented town of Fenmore
factor-demand-supply-s3.html: Fenmore has a large market for nurses. During one year: (1) the town's population ages and hospitals treat more patients; (2) a nearby city raises its nurses' pay well above Fenmore's; (3) Fenmore's hospitals buy monitoring equipment that lets each nurse care for more patients; (4) a new nursing school in Fenmore graduates its first large class.

competitive-factor-markets-s2.title: Workers or kiln time at Ortolan Ceramics
competitive-factor-markets-s2.html: Ortolan Ceramics (invented) makes bowls with workers and rented kiln time, and it buys both in competitive markets. The last worker-hour it uses adds 40 bowls and costs $20. The last hour of kiln time adds 90 bowls and costs $30. The owner wants to make the same number of bowls at the lowest cost.

monopsony-s3.title: A minimum wage for Caddock County nurses
monopsony-s3.html: Use the Caddock County table. The county sets a minimum wage of $14 an hour for nurses. The hospital may pay more but not less. At $14 an hour, up to 4 nurses are willing to work; a fifth would need $16.

items.q: Use the table. What is the marginal product of the third worker, in candles per day?

mistakes.why: 25 is the average product of three workers (75 ÷ 3). Marginal product is the change in output from the third worker alone: 75 - 55.
75 is total product with three workers. The third worker adds only the change: 75 - 55 = 20.

items.q: Use the table. What is the marginal revenue product of the fourth worker, in dollars per day?

mistakes.why: $180 is the revenue from all four workers' output (90 × $2). MRP uses the fourth worker's marginal product only: 15 × $2.
15 is the marginal product in candles. Multiply by the marginal revenue of a candle, $2, to get dollars.

items.q: In the table, why does each added worker bring in less revenue than the one before?
options: The price of candles falls as the firm hires more workers
Later workers are paid a lower wage than earlier ones
Each worker adds fewer candles at the same $2 price
Total product falls after the second worker

items.q: Use the table. The market price of candles rises from $2 to $3. What is the new marginal revenue product of the second worker, in dollars per day?

mistakes.why: $50 is the MRP at the old price. A higher product price raises every worker's MRP: use $3.
$165 uses total product with two workers. MRP uses the second worker's marginal product, 25 candles.

items.q: In the scenario, why do the boatyards want more welders?
options: Buyers want more boats, and welders' work is needed to build them
Welders have decided to work more hours this year
The boatyards earn revenue from selling welding services to crews
A welder is a good that households buy for their own use

items.q: In the scenario, in which market do the boatyards buy welders' work, and who sells it?
options: A product market, where households sell finished boats to the boatyards
A product market, where firms sell labor to households
A factor market, where firms sell boats to fishing crews
A factor market, where households sell their labor to firms

items.q: In the scenario, which later event would most likely lead the boatyards to want fewer welders?
options: More fishing crews move to Brackwater
The fish-processing plant closes and crews order fewer boats
The price of a new fishing boat rises
Welders find new tools that let them weld faster

items.q: Use the table. What is Firm Y's marginal revenue product of the third worker, in dollars?

mistakes.why: $40 multiplies by $10, a price taker's marginal revenue. Firm Y must cut its price to sell more, so each extra unit adds only its own marginal revenue, $6.
$60 multiplies marginal revenue by price. MRP is marginal product times marginal revenue: 4 × $6.

items.q: Use the table. What is Firm X's marginal revenue product of the second worker, in dollars?

mistakes.why: $40 uses Firm Y's marginal revenue. Firm X sells every unit at $10, so its MR is $10.
11 adds two marginal products. MRP is one worker's marginal product times marginal revenue: 5 × $10.

items.q: Use the table. Why does Firm Y's MRP fall faster than Firm X's as each firm adds workers?
options: Firm Y's workers have a smaller marginal product than Firm X's
Firm Y's marginal revenue falls as well as its marginal product
Firm X can charge a higher price than Firm Y for each unit
Firm X's marginal revenue rises as it sells more units

items.q: What is a factor market?
options: A market where households buy finished goods from firms
A market where a government sets the price of each input
A market where firms sell goods to other countries
A market where firms buy labor, land and capital from their owners

items.q: Why is the demand for a factor of production called a derived demand?
options: Buyers want the product that the factor helps make
The factor's price is figured out by a formula set by the firm
Workers derive satisfaction from the goods they make
The factor's demand curve is drawn from the firm's total cost

items.q: A firm sells its output in a perfectly competitive market. Which expression gives the marginal revenue product of a worker?
options: Marginal revenue × price
Total product × price
Marginal product × price
Marginal product ÷ price

items.q: Why is a firm's MRP curve its demand curve for labor?
options: It shows how many people want to work at each wage
It shows the firm's total cost of hiring each number of workers
It shows how much output each worker makes on average
It shows what each added worker is worth to the firm

items.q: A new machine lets each of a firm's workers produce more output. The product price does not change. What happens to the MRP of each worker?
options: It falls, because the machine replaces some workers
It rises, because each worker's marginal product rises
It stays the same, because the price of the product is unchanged
It rises, because the price of the product rises

items.q: Hiring one more worker raises a firm's output by 8 units. Each extra unit adds $5 to the firm's revenue. What is that worker's marginal revenue product, in dollars?

mistakes.why: 13 adds the two numbers. MRP multiplies the extra output by the extra revenue per unit: 8 × $5.
1.6 divides. MRP is marginal product times marginal revenue.

items.q: Put the links in order: buyers start wanting more bicycles, and a bike maker hires more assemblers.
options: Demand for bicycles increases
The price of bicycles rises
Each assembler's MRP rises (MP × the higher price)
The bike maker wants to hire more assemblers at each wage

items.q: Which of these are payments made in a factor market? Select all that apply.
options: Wages a garage pays its mechanics
Rent a farmer pays for a field
The price a shopper pays for a loaf of bread
A shoe store's revenue from selling sneakers
A sales tax paid on a new phone

items.q: Which of these is a transaction in a factor market?
options: A student buys a coffee at the café
A café sells gift cards to customers
A café hires a weekend barista
A family buys a used car from a neighbor

items.q: The price of a good falls, and nothing else changes. What happens to the marginal revenue product of the workers who make it?
options: It falls at every quantity of labor
It rises, because the good is cheaper to make
It stays the same, because marginal product is unchanged
It falls for the first worker and rises for the others

items.q: Builders in an invented region win many new orders for houses. On the graph of the market for carpenters, shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: more demand for houses, which raises carpenters' MRP

slips.SL: Carpenters have not changed how willing they are to work; it is the builders who want more carpenters, so labor demand shifts.

items.q: A new rule requires every electrician to complete an extra year of training before working. On the graph of the market for electricians, shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: a training rule that cuts the number of qualified electricians

slips.DL: The rule changes who can work, the sellers of labor. Firms' demand for electricians has not changed.

items.q: Grocery stores install self-checkout machines that do the work of cashiers, and the machines become much cheaper. On the graph of the market for cashiers, shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

slips.SL: Cashiers' willingness to work is unchanged; the stores want fewer of them, so labor demand shifts.

items.q: Many young adults move to an invented city, and most of them look for restaurant jobs. On the graph of the market for restaurant workers, shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

key.because: more people looking for restaurant work

items.q: The graph shows a change in the market for app developers. Which event could have caused it?
options: More students graduate with app-building skills
Developers become more productive with better software tools
Fewer people buy apps, so the price of apps falls
Other tech jobs start paying much higher wages

items.q: In the graph, what happens to the wage and the number of developers hired?
options: Both fall
The wage falls and the number hired rises
The wage rises and the number hired falls
Both rise

items.q: In the graph, a single firm that hires developers pays the new wage set in the market. How does the firm's own MRP curve compare with before?
options: It is unchanged, because the firm makes the same number of apps
It has shifted right, because the wage is now lower
It has become horizontal at the new wage
It has shifted left, because each developer's work brings in less revenue

items.q: Use the table. Before online orders rise, what are the equilibrium wage and number of warehouse workers?
options: $20 and 450 workers
$18 and 400 workers
$14 and 500 workers
$22 and 500 workers

items.q: Use the table. After online orders rise, the wage is still $18 for a while. How many more workers do warehouses want at $18 than are willing to work?

items.q: Use the table. After online orders rise, what are the new equilibrium wage and number of workers?
options: $18 and 500 workers
$20 and 450 workers
$22 and 500 workers
$18 and 400 workers

items.q: In the scenario, how does event (2), higher pay for nurses in the nearby city, affect the market for nurses in Fenmore?
options: Labor demand in Fenmore increases
Labor supply in Fenmore increases
Nothing changes, because Fenmore's wage is the same
Labor supply in Fenmore decreases

items.q: In the scenario, which events shift the demand for nurses in Fenmore? Select all that apply.
options: (1) more patients in hospitals
(2) higher pay in the nearby city
(3) equipment that makes each nurse more productive
(4) a large class of new nurses

items.q: In the scenario, events (1) and (4) happen together. What can you say about the equilibrium in Fenmore's market for nurses?
options: Employment rises, and the wage change is indeterminate
The wage rises, and the employment change is indeterminate
The wage and employment both rise for certain
The wage falls and employment is unchanged

items.q: In the scenario, event (4) happens alone. What happens to the wage and employment of nurses in Fenmore?
options: The wage rises and employment rises
The wage falls and employment falls
The wage falls and employment rises
The wage rises and employment falls

items.q: Put the links in order: the demand for solar panels rises, and the market for panel installers changes.
options: The price of solar panel installations rises
Each installer's MRP rises (MP × the higher price)
The demand for installers (DL) shifts right
The wage of installers and the number hired both rise

items.q: A country raises the minimum age at which people may work in factories. What happens in the market for factory workers?
options: Labor demand shifts left: the wage and employment fall
Labor supply shifts right: the wage falls and employment rises
Labor demand shifts right: the wage and employment rise
Labor supply shifts left: the wage rises and employment falls

items.q: On a graph of the market for plumbers, how is a higher wage shown when nothing else about the market has changed?
options: Labor supply shifts right
A movement along labor supply and labor demand, not a shift of either
Labor demand shifts left
Both curves shift left

items.q: Delivery drones and drivers are complements for a parcel company: each drone needs a driver to load it. Drones become much cheaper. What happens to the demand for drivers?
options: It decreases
It does not change
It increases
Labor supply decreases instead

items.q: Which of these would shift the labor supply curve for truck drivers to the right? Select all that apply.
options: A cheaper, shorter path to a commercial driver's license
Higher pay in warehouse jobs that drivers could take
Safer trucks that make the job less stressful
A rise in the demand for shipping
A rise in drivers' wages

items.q: The price of a machine that does the same job as forklift operators falls sharply. Assume warehouses replace operators with the machines. What happens to the wage and employment of forklift operators?
options: Both fall
Both rise
The wage rises and employment falls
The wage falls and employment rises

items.q: Label the side-by-side graphs of a perfectly competitive labor market and one firm that hires in it: both pairs of axes, the market curves, the firm's MRP curve and the firm's labor supply line.
On the firm's graph, draw the firm's labor supply (marginal factor cost) line at the right height.

slips.MRP: MRP is the firm's demand for labor. The firm's supply line is horizontal at the wage the market sets.

items.q: On the firm's graph, mark the number of workers the firm hires to maximize profit.
A new law limits the hours each worker in this industry may work, so fewer hours of labor are offered at each wage. Shift the right curve in the labor market, then draw the firm's new wage line.

key.because: a law that cuts the hours of labor offered

slips.DL: The law changes how much labor is offered, the supply side; firms' demand is unchanged.

items.q: In the same industry, many new firms open and hire this kind of worker, while one existing firm's MRP does not change. Shift the right curve in the labor market and mark how many workers the existing firm now hires.

key.because: more firms hiring this kind of worker

items.q: Use the table. What is the marginal revenue product of the fifth carpenter, in dollars per week?

mistakes.why: $720 is the revenue from all five carpenters' chairs. MRP uses the fifth carpenter's marginal product: 5 chairs.
$120 is the fourth carpenter's MRP (6 chairs). The fifth adds 36 - 31 = 5.

items.q: Use the table. The market wage is $110 per week. How many carpenters does the workshop hire to maximize profit?

mistakes.why: Every carpenter adds some revenue, but the fifth and sixth add less than the $110 they cost. Stop at the last one whose MRP is at least the wage.
The fifth carpenter's MRP is $100, below the $110 wage, so hiring her lowers profit.

items.q: Use the table. The market wage rises from $110 to $130 per week. How many carpenters does the workshop now hire?
Use the table. The workshop's rent rises by $500 a week, a fixed cost. The wage stays at $110. What happens to the number of carpenters it hires?
options: It stays at 4: rent changes neither MRP nor MRC
It falls to 3, so the workshop can save on total costs
It rises to 5, to cover the higher rent
It falls to 0, because profit is lower

items.q: In the scenario, what is the marginal product per dollar of labor, in bowls per dollar?

mistakes.why: 0.5 divides the wage by MP. Put the marginal product on top: bowls per dollar.
800 multiplies. The rule compares output per dollar spent, MP ÷ price.

items.q: In the scenario, how should Ortolan change its mix of inputs to make the same output at a lower cost?
options: Use more worker-hours and less kiln time
Keep the mix, because a kiln hour adds more bowls than a worker-hour
Keep the mix, because the kiln costs more per hour than a worker
Use more kiln time and fewer worker-hours

items.q: In the scenario, Ortolan rents more kiln time and uses fewer worker-hours. What happens to the two "per dollar" numbers as it does?
options: Both rise, because the cost of making each bowl falls
Kiln time's falls and labor's rises, until they are equal
Kiln time's rises and labor's falls
Neither changes, because the prices of both inputs are fixed

items.q: Suppose the bowls sell for $1 each, so each input's MRP equals its MP in dollars. Ortolan adjusts until labor and kiln time each give 1.5 bowls per dollar. Is it maximizing profit?
options: Yes: the two ratios are equal, so profit is already as large as it can be
No: each input adds more than it costs, so it should use more of both
No: it should use less of both inputs
Yes: any ratio above 1 means the firm earns a profit

items.q: Why is a firm in a perfectly competitive labor market called a wage taker?
options: It pays each worker the value of that worker's output
It takes a share of each worker's wage as profit
It sets the wage where its MRP is highest
It is too small a buyer of labor to change the wage

items.q: What is the profit-maximizing hiring rule for any firm?
options: Hire until marginal revenue product equals marginal resource cost
Hire until total revenue equals total cost
Hire until marginal product is at its highest
Hire until average product equals the wage

items.q: A firm's total labor cost is $180 with 2 workers and $270 with 3 workers. What is the marginal resource cost of the third worker, in dollars?

mistakes.why: $30 divides the $90 change by 3 workers. The change in workers is 1 (from 2 to 3), so divide by 1.
$270 is the total cost of three workers. MRC is the change from adding the third: 270 - 180.

items.q: A competitive firm's next worker has an MRP of $95. The market wage is $80. What should the firm do?
options: Not hire, because her MRP is below the MRP of earlier workers
Hire if the firm's total revenue is above its total cost
Hire her: she adds $15 more to revenue than to cost
Hire her and pay her a wage of $95, her MRP

items.q: A perfectly competitive firm sells in a competitive product market and hires in a competitive labor market. Which changes would lead it to hire more workers? Select all that apply.
options: A rise in the price of its product
New equipment that raises each worker's output
A rise in the rent on its building
A rise in the market wage
A fall in the price of its product

items.q: A competitive firm's workers have MRPs of $70, $60, $50, $40 and $30. The market wage is $50. How many workers does it hire?

mistakes.why: The third worker's MRP equals the wage, so hiring her does not lower profit; by the MRP = MRC rule the firm hires 3.
The fourth and fifth workers add less than the $50 they cost.

items.q: Why does a firm's marginal factor cost of labor equal the wage when the labor market is perfectly competitive?
options: The firm pays each worker the MRP of that worker
Each added worker produces as much as the one before
The wage falls as the firm hires more workers
Each added worker is hired at the same market wage

items.q: Label the monopsony graph: both axes and all three curves.
Mark the point that shows the number of workers the monopsonist hires and the wage it pays.

slips.MFC: The crossing of MRP and MFC gives the quantity hired, but the wage is read down on the labor supply curve.

items.q: Shade the monopsonist's wage bill.
Shade the deadweight loss that results from the monopsony.
A minimum wage is set equal to the wage that a competitive labor market would reach. Draw the minimum wage line at that height.
The graph shows a minimum wage set above the monopsony wage and below the competitive wage. Mark the number of workers the firm now hires at the minimum wage.
In the graph, which area is the wage bill the employer pays?
options: Area b
Areas a and b
Area a
The area under MRP out to the number hired

items.q: In the graph, which area is the deadweight loss caused by the monopsony?
options: Area b
Area a
Areas a and b
There is no deadweight loss

items.q: In the graph, compared with a perfectly competitive labor market with the same MRP and SL curves, the monopsony
options: hires fewer workers and pays a higher wage
hires more workers and pays a lower wage
hires the same number of workers and pays a lower wage
hires fewer workers and pays a lower wage

items.q: Use the table. What is the marginal factor cost of the third nurse, in dollars per hour?

mistakes.why: $12 is the wage. For a single employer, MFC is above the wage: the new nurse's $12 plus $2 more for each of the two nurses already hired.
$36 is the total labor cost of three nurses. MFC is the change: $36 - $20.

items.q: Use the table. How many nurses does the hospital hire to maximize profit?

mistakes.why: 4 compares MRP with the wage, as a wage taker would. A single employer compares MRP with MFC, which is higher than the wage.
The fourth and fifth nurses add less to revenue than to the hospital's labor cost.

items.q: Use the table. What hourly wage does the hospital pay at the profit-maximizing number of nurses?
Use the table. What is the hospital's wage bill per hour at the profit-maximizing number of nurses, in dollars?

mistakes.why: $48 uses the MFC as the wage. Each nurse is paid $12, read from labor supply.
$66 uses the MRP as the wage. Pay comes from labor supply: $12 × 3.

items.q: In the scenario, what is the hospital's marginal factor cost of the second, third and fourth nurses after the minimum wage?
options: $12, $16 and $20, as before
$14 each, because every nurse already earns $14
$10, $12 and $14, the wages in the table
$26, $22 and $18, their MRPs

items.q: In the scenario, how many nurses does the hospital hire after the minimum wage?
options: 3, the same as before
2, down from 3
5, up from 3
4, up from 3

items.q: In the scenario, what happens to nurses' wage and employment compared with no minimum wage?
options: Both rise, to $14 and 4 nurses
The wage rises and employment falls
The wage rises and employment stays at 3
Both fall

items.q: What is a monopsony?
options: A market with a single seller of a product
A labor market with many employers that each take the wage
A market with a single buyer, such as one employer of a kind of labor
A firm that hires workers in many different towns

items.q: Why does a monopsonist's MFC curve lie above the labor supply curve?
options: It pays each new worker more than the workers already hired
Its workers produce more output than workers elsewhere
It pays each worker the worker's MRP
To hire one more worker it must raise the wage for every worker

items.q: A single employer pays 10 workers $15 an hour. To hire an 11th worker it must raise the wage to $16 for all 11. What is the MFC of the 11th worker, in dollars per hour?

mistakes.why: $16 is the new wage. The added cost also includes the $1 raise for the 10 workers already hired.
$176 is the new total labor cost. MFC is the change: $176 - $150.

items.q: In a perfectly competitive labor market, a minimum wage is set above the equilibrium wage. How does its effect on employment differ from a minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage in a monopsony?
options: It raises employment, like the one in the monopsony
It lowers employment; the monopsony one raises it
Both lower employment
Neither changes employment

items.q: The price of the product made by a monopsonist's workers rises. Shift the right curve and mark the new number of workers hired and the wage paid.

key.because: a higher price for the product the workers make
